edition.deck: A new investigation traces Channel crossings to a German boat dealer; fresh documents raise questions over Peter Mandelson’s time as ambassador, while Denmark faces a growing list of domestic stories.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritises significant new reporting and developments from the day. Stories already prominent in the morning edition are not repeated without a meaningful new development. Danish coverage focuses on fresh reporting, including pollution concerns, public services and climate risks.

content.headline: Iranian strike in Kuwait kills two Italian technicians, Italy says
content.shortHeadline: Two Italian technicians killed in strike on Kuwait site
content.standfirst: Italy says the two men worked for arms manufacturer Rheinmetall at an air-defence site. Kuwait said four people were injured by shrapnel after Iranian drones were detected and intercepted.

image.caption: A Rheinmetall site in Kuwait targeted in the strike, according to Italian and Kuwaiti authorities.

sources.originalTitle: Two Italians killed after Iranian strike in Kuwait

segments.body: Two Italian technicians have been killed after an Iranian strike on a site in Kuwait, Italy’s foreign ministry says. The men worked for German arms manufacturer Rheinmetall, carrying out maintenance on systems used by Kuwait’s armed forces, Italian news agency Ansa reported.

segments.title: Regional tensions
segments.body: Kuwait’s defence ministry earlier said four people, including the two Italians, had been injured by falling shrapnel after drones from Iran were detected and intercepted. The strike comes amid renewed exchanges of fire between the US and Iran and stalled negotiations.

content.headline: German boat dealer suspected of supplying Channel smuggling gangs
content.shortHeadline: German boat dealer suspected of supplying Channel gangs
content.standfirst: Investigators allege that boats or engines from a western German firm featured in nearly a third of detected Channel crossings in the first four months of 2026. Its managing director is contesting extradition to France.

image.caption: The BBC confronts German boat dealer Marvin Reuter at his business.

sources.originalTitle: German boat dealer suspected of supplying Channel smuggling gangs, BBC finds

segments.body: European authorities suspect German boat dealer Marvin Reuter of supplying equipment to people-smuggling networks. Files reviewed by the BBC say boats or engines linked to his firm, MaReBoote, were involved in 29% of detected Channel crossings up to the end of April. Reuter is contesting extradition to France, where he could face charges; he has not been formally charged and is presumed innocent.

segments.title: Evidence and unanswered questions
segments.body: French investigators say at least 82 boats from the firm reached the English coast in just over two years. The case also draws on alleged accomplices’ accounts, covert jail recordings and two fatal crossing attempts in which investigators suspect the firm’s equipment was involved. Reuter did not address the allegations when approached by the BBC and accused it of harassment.

segments.title: A cross-border investigation
segments.body: French prosecutors say selling boats is legal unless a seller knows they will be used by smuggling or trafficking networks. Reuter’s lawyers have challenged extradition, arguing that allegations should be heard in Germany. The investigation follows a change in German law that made aiding smuggling to the UK explicitly illegal at the end of 2025.

content.headline: Women in Iran face death sentences after protests, rights advocates warn
content.shortHeadline: Rights advocates warn of more death sentences for women in Iran
content.standfirst: A UN rapporteur identified six women sentenced to death in connection with January’s protests, while rights groups say more women have faced capital charges this year. Iran rejects allegations of torture and says the cases involve serious crimes.

image.caption: Twin sisters Taraneh and Romina Rahimi, who their cousin says were arrested after joining protests.

sources.originalTitle: Desperate appeals from women on death row in Iran after protests

segments.body: Women arrested after protests in Iran are among those facing death sentences, according to UN rapporteur Mai Sato and human rights groups. The BBC reports on the case of Taraneh Rahimi, 21, whose cousin says she was beaten in custody and signed a confession after threats against her twin sister. The BBC says it has seen part of a sentencing document; court documents have not been published.

segments.title: Disputed accounts
segments.body: Sato says six women were sentenced to death this year in connection with the January protests, and identifies three further women sentenced in other cases. Amnesty International describes several cases as politically motivated. Iran’s embassy in London rejects claims of torture and says death sentences relate to offences such as intentional murder or taking up arms.

segments.title: What remains unclear
segments.body: At least 39 people have been executed in connection with the January protests, Sato says. She is concerned that some death sentences overturned by courts may later be reimposed. The BBC notes that official details are often limited and some cases may go unreported; two of the three overturned sentences it describes were sent for retrial.

content.headline: Diesel tanker capsizes near Ibiza, killing one crew member
content.shortHeadline: One dead after diesel tanker capsizes near Ibiza
content.standfirst: The Malta-flagged Med Emre was carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel when it capsized off Ibiza. All 17 crew were rescued, but one later died; the scale of any fuel spill is still unknown.

image.caption: The Med Emre capsized off Ibiza; Spain sent a pollution-control vessel to assess possible environmental damage.

source.credit: CGT Mar y Puertos via Reuters

sources.originalTitle: Diesel tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes capsizes near Ibiza, killing one

segments.body: One crew member has died after the Med Emre, a chemical tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel, capsized 25 nautical miles off Ibiza. All 17 crew were rescued, with seven taken to hospital; six were reported to have minor injuries. The vessel is partially submerged, Spanish authorities say.

segments.title: Environmental impact still being assessed
segments.body: Spain’s maritime rescue service is using an aircraft and pollution-control vessel to assess possible environmental damage. There is still little information about whether fuel has leaked, the president of the Balearic Islands said. The cause of the capsize has not been established.

content.headline: Cheaper HIV-prevention injection begins reaching African countries
content.shortHeadline: Lower-cost HIV prevention jab starts reaching Africa
content.standfirst: A generic version of lenacapavir, given twice a year, has arrived in Zambia, with Uganda expected to receive supplies soon. The Global Fund says the cheaper medicine could widen access to prevention across the region.

image.caption: Lenacapavir is used as an injection to prevent HIV infection.

sources.originalTitle: Hope for millions as cheaper HIV prevention jab reaches Africa

segments.body: The first global shipment of a lower-cost generic version of lenacapavir has arrived in Zambia, and deliveries to Uganda are expected in the coming days, the Global Fund says. The twice-yearly injection is used to prevent HIV infection and is expected to cost about $40 per person annually.

segments.title: Expanding access
segments.body: In a trial involving more than 5,000 adolescent girls and young women in Uganda and South Africa, none of those given the injection contracted HIV. The World Health Organization recommended lenacapavir for HIV prevention in 2025. The Global Fund expects 24 countries to receive supplies by the end of this year and aims, with the US government, to reach at least three million people by the end of 2028.

segments.title: The funding challenge
segments.body: The original medicine developed by Gilead Sciences cost about $28,000 a year in the US. The rollout comes as concerns grow that US foreign-aid cuts could undermine progress against HIV in African countries that depend heavily on international funding.

content.headline: Thanksgiving storms disrupt US flights as millions prepare to travel
content.shortHeadline: Storms disrupt Thanksgiving travel across the US
content.standfirst: More than 350 flights were cancelled and about 700 delayed on Thursday as storms threatened both US coasts during one of the country’s busiest travel periods. New York’s Thanksgiving parade has been postponed.

image.caption: Storms threaten travel across North America during the Thanksgiving holiday.

sources.originalTitle: Hundreds of flights cancelled as severe weather disrupts Thanksgiving travel in US

segments.body: More than 350 flights in the US were cancelled and another 700 delayed on Thursday, according to FlightAware, as severe weather coincided with Thanksgiving travel. More than 80 million people were expected to travel during the holiday period, and the Federal Aviation Administration had warned of delays through the week.

segments.title: Risks on both coasts
segments.body: The National Weather Service forecast heavy rain, high winds and coastal flooding on the eastern seaboard, while Pacific storms were expected to bring rain, mountain snow and strong winds in the west. New Jersey’s governor declared a state of emergency, and organisers postponed New York’s Macy’s Thanksgiving parade until Saturday.

segments.title: Separate airport investigation
segments.body: The FAA is investigating after a FedEx aircraft overran a runway at Miami International Airport on Wednesday. No injuries were reported. The incident briefly grounded flights to the airport and left some travel delays there, according to the report.

content.headline: France’s political centre struggles to find a presidential contender
content.shortHeadline: France’s political centre lacks a clear 2027 candidate
content.standfirst: With Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon leading polls, centrist and traditional parties remain divided over candidates and strategy. Analysts say that fragmentation could make a second-round contest between the two more likely.

sources.originalTitle: France's political mainstream risks presidential vote debacle with no clear candidate

segments.body: France’s political mainstream has no clear presidential candidate five months before the first round of the 2027 election, the BBC reports. Polls show hard-right leader Marine Le Pen and left-wing France Unbowed leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon dominating, while centrist and traditional parties struggle to agree on a contender or shared platform.

segments.title: A divided centre-right
segments.body: Former prime minister Édouard Philippe has lost ground in recent polls, while other figures—including Gabriel Attal, Bruno Retailleau and Cannes mayor David Lisnard—are also seeking the centre-right’s support. Political commentators cited by the BBC say the crowded field and lack of a common programme weaken the challenge.

segments.title: The left’s shifting alliances
segments.body: On the left, European Parliament member Raphaël Glucksmann has been discussed as a possible candidate, but several figures and groups have moved towards Mélenchon. The BBC’s analysis says it remains possible for a mainstream candidate to emerge, but the far-right and far-left have a substantial head start.

content.headline: Jihadist groups turn to local alliances, but their ambitions remain uncertain
content.shortHeadline: Jihadist groups focus locally, but their aims remain unclear
content.standfirst: Some al-Qaeda-linked movements are emphasising local issues and building alliances as they seek influence, while Islamic State remains committed to global jihad. Analysts disagree on whether this is a change in purpose or a shift in tactics.

sources.originalTitle: Has global jihadism failed, or is it simply changing shape?

segments.body: Some jihadist groups are putting greater emphasis on local power and community support rather than attacks on the West, the BBC’s analysis finds. In Somalia, al-Shabab has publicised food distribution; in Mali, al-Qaeda-linked JNIM has presented itself as a defender of ordinary people and joined forces with Tuareg separatists.

segments.title: Alliances and political pragmatism
segments.body: The BBC describes parallels with Syria’s new president, Ahmed al-Sharaa, who broke with al-Qaeda and Islamic State and built local alliances before taking power. JNIM and al-Shabab have also shown signs of compromise, but analysts say it is too early to know whether they will follow that path or how far they are prepared to go.

segments.title: Tactics or a lasting shift?
segments.body: Some experts see pragmatic alliances as a way to gain power while preserving longer-term aims of imposing strict interpretations of Islamic law. Islamic State remains hostile to compromise, and al-Qaeda’s Yemen branch continues to call for attacks on Western and Israeli targets. The groups’ ambitions remain unresolved.

content.headline: New documents show Mandelson kept shares while serving as US ambassador
content.shortHeadline: Mandelson kept firm shares while serving as ambassador
content.standfirst: Documents released by the government show Peter Mandelson retained shares in his lobbying firm Global Counsel and consulted former colleagues on his work as ambassador. The Metropolitan Police investigation into alleged misconduct remains ongoing.

image.caption: Peter Mandelson leaves his London home after the release of documents about his appointment as US ambassador.

sources.originalTitle: Mandelson kept shares as ambassador despite conflict of interest fears, documents show
Mandelson tried to set up meeting between Trump adviser and lobbying firm he held shares in

segments.body: Newly released documents show Lord Mandelson still held shares in Global Counsel six months after becoming US ambassador, despite civil servants’ concerns about a perceived conflict of interest. He kept the shares until February 2026, when the company went into administration. Mandelson has not commented on this latest release; no charges have been brought against him.

segments.title: Questions over his official work
segments.body: While still a shareholder, Mandelson sought to arrange an “under the radar” lunch between a Global Counsel employee and an economic adviser to Donald Trump, according to the documents. He also sought advice from the firm on a speech about Britain’s role in the world. The Foreign Office had warned him to avoid any perception of advancing the firm’s commercial interests.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s report details the proposed lunch on alternatives to the World Trade Organization and says key documents—including Mandelson’s conflict-of-interest declaration and material on his security clearance—remain withheld.

segments.title: Reviews and investigation
segments.body: Security minister Dan Jarvis said the government plans to strengthen its conflicts-of-interest policy. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he would address political reform in a 10-year plan. The Metropolitan Police says its investigation into alleged misconduct in public office is ongoing; the released documents do not establish that Mandelson committed a crime.

content.headline: UK retailers investigate after faulty goods are found on Ghana dump
content.shortHeadline: Faulty UK appliances found at Ghana e-waste site
content.standfirst: An investigation found returned appliances linked to major UK retailers at a waste site in Accra, where workers burn and dismantle electronics without protective equipment. The retailers named say they are investigating or auditing suppliers.

image.caption: Aerial view of waste dumps in Ghana.

sources.originalTitle: Faulty electrical goods returned to UK supermarkets ending up on Ghana ‘megadump’

segments.body: Faulty electrical goods bearing labels linked to Tesco and Argos were found at Agbogbloshie, a major e-waste site in Accra, a joint investigation by Unearthed and Greenpeace Africa reports. Items included toasters and slow cookers. The investigation says workers burn and dismantle appliances there, often without gloves or masks.

segments.title: How goods may have travelled
segments.body: UK rules generally prohibit exporting broken electrical goods to Africa. The investigation says returned items can enter liquidation sales as “untested returns”, then be bought in bulk and shipped overseas. The Environment Agency says exported electrical waste must be notified and approved, and that it uses intelligence to investigate suspicious shipments.

segments.title: Retailer responses
segments.body: Tesco says it has suspended its third-party electronic-waste providers while it audits them. Argos says it is investigating how the goods arrived in Ghana. The investigation also found British returns for sale in local second-hand shops; it does not establish who exported each item or whether a particular retailer broke the law.

content.headline: Labour MPs urge Burnham to block Rosebank oilfield approval
content.shortHeadline: Nearly 100 Labour MPs press Burnham to oppose Rosebank
content.standfirst: A letter signed by 92 backbenchers and at least four frontbenchers urges the prime minister not to approve the North Sea project. The dispute exposes a deep party divide over jobs, energy security and climate commitments.

image.caption: Opponents of the Rosebank oilfield protest outside the Treasury in London.

sources.originalTitle: Labour’s split over Rosebank oilfield exposed by letter from nearly 100 MPs

segments.body: Ninety-two Labour backbenchers and at least four frontbenchers have urged Prime Minister Andy Burnham not to approve the Rosebank oilfield, in a letter reported by the Guardian. The project is the UK’s biggest undeveloped offshore field and has become a test of the government’s climate policy.

segments.title: A dispute over emissions and returns
segments.body: Opponents say most of the oil would be exported and that approval would add an estimated one million tonnes of carbon dioxide by 2042. Supporters, including some cabinet colleagues and trade unions, point to about 500 jobs and potential tax revenues of up to £500m a year. The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, is understood to be leaning against approval.

segments.title: The decision ahead
segments.body: Ministers approved the smaller Jackdaw gasfield last month, arguing that its energy-security benefits would offset added emissions. Fahnbulleh has said the same case would not apply to Rosebank. Burnham says the decision is hers, but Labour MPs opposing the project want him to back her if she rejects it.

content.headline: Man found guilty of seven attempted murders in LNER train stabbing
content.shortHeadline: Train attacker found guilty of seven attempted murders
content.standfirst: A jury convicted Anthony Williams over attacks on passengers on a London-bound train in 2025. It is still considering seven other attempted-murder counts; the defence said he was experiencing acute psychosis.

image.caption: CCTV footage shown to jurors showed Anthony Williams holding a knife on an LNER train.

sources.originalTitle: Man found guilty of attempted murder of seven people on LNER train

segments.body: Anthony Williams has been found guilty of seven counts of attempted murder for stabbing passengers on an LNER train travelling from Doncaster to London in November 2025. The jury is still considering seven further counts after a six-week trial at Cambridge crown court.

segments.title: The case heard in court
segments.body: Williams admitted stabbing 14 people over two days but denied the attempted-murder charges. The court heard that he had acute psychosis related to schizophrenia at the time. The prosecution described a “storm of violence” on a busy train; the defence argued he did not intend to kill and was acting under delusions.

content.headline: UK commits £9.5m to windfarm project for war-hit Ukraine
content.shortHeadline: UK to invest £9.5m in Ukrainian windfarm
content.standfirst: The proposed 200-megawatt project is intended to supply power for about 300,000 households as Russian attacks damage Ukraine’s energy system. Its location has not been disclosed.

image.caption: The Tyligulska windfarm in southern Ukraine, built during the war.

sources.originalTitle: UK to invest £9.5m in Ukraine windfarm to bolster war-hit energy system

segments.body: The UK will invest £9.5m in a 200-megawatt windfarm in Ukraine, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband says. The project, expected to be built and operated by UK-registered Elementum Energy, is intended to provide enough electricity for about 300,000 homes. Its location has not been disclosed.

segments.title: Rebuilding a damaged energy system
segments.body: Kyiv says Russian strikes have damaged or destroyed more than 80% of Ukraine’s pre-war power-generation capacity. The UK government says it has offered more than £770m for energy-system recovery, including emergency support and longer-term investment in renewable and nuclear generation.

segments.title: Winter pressure
segments.body: The announcement follows renewed Russian attacks on energy infrastructure. A strike on a thermal power plant near Odesa on Wednesday caused power, heating and water outages in parts of the city, according to the report. Ukraine has installed more than 3GW of renewable capacity since Russia’s full-scale invasion, it says.

content.headline: UK publishes post-Brexit food and emissions treaty details
content.shortHeadline: UK publishes details of two EU reset treaties
content.standfirst: The food-trade and emissions agreements are being published alongside legislation to implement them. A reported 10-year exit clause and powers to align with evolving EU rules have drawn criticism from opposition parties.

image.caption: Andy Burnham meets EU leaders Ursula von der Leyen and António Costa in Brussels.

sources.originalTitle: Details of two treaties at heart of Andy Burnham’s EU reset to be published

segments.body: The UK government is publishing the legal texts of its food-trade and emissions-trading agreements with the EU, alongside a bill to implement them in UK law. The deals were agreed at last week’s summit; the youth-mobility agreement is not among the two texts being published now.

segments.title: What the bill would allow
segments.body: The legislation would let the government align UK rules with EU single-market rules in areas covered by the food deal, including changes to rules as they evolve. The Guardian reports that the bill would allow some changes to be made without a full parliamentary vote each time.

segments.title: Exit clause and criticism
segments.body: The agreements are reported to include a 10-year termination clause that could require a party ending a deal to contribute to rebuilding border-check infrastructure. Opposition leaders have criticised the terms. The government says the agreements should reduce paperwork and make trade with the UK’s largest trading partner cheaper and easier.

content.headline: UK youth unemployment measure falls, but 959,000 remain out of work or study
content.shortHeadline: 959,000 young people in UK are not working or studying
content.standfirst: The number of 16- to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training fell by 22,000 in the three months to September, but remains close to a decade high. The number of 16- and 17-year-olds in the group rose.

image.caption: The government is preparing its response to recommendations on young people and work.

sources.originalTitle: Number of Neets in UK falls below a million as Burnham pushes to tackle crisis

segments.body: There were 959,000 people aged 16 to 24 in the UK not in education, employment or training in the three months to September, Office for National Statistics figures show. The total fell by 22,000 from the previous quarter but was 17,000 higher than a year earlier and remains close to a decade high.

segments.title: Different trends by age
segments.body: The decline was driven by a fall among 18- to 24-year-olds, whose number in the group reached 867,000. For 16- and 17-year-olds, the total rose to 92,000, the highest since 2012. One in eight young people were not in education, work or training in the latest quarter.

segments.title: Policy response ahead
segments.body: The figures come as the government prepares a response to Alan Milburn’s review of youth employment. Ministers say they are developing a new support system; a white paper on welfare reform is expected next year. A youth-employment charity says even six months out of work can harm wellbeing.

content.headline: Danish authority warns plastic may have reached fields from pig feed
content.shortHeadline: Plastic from pig feed may have spread on Danish fields
content.standfirst: The food authority says there is a high risk that slurry containing plastic contaminated fields at a major pig producer. The company also told inspectors it spread plastic-contaminated feed on a field after being ordered not to use it.

image.caption: A pig herd at a farm in Lejre where inspectors found plastic in feed handling.

sources.originalTitle: Fødevarestyrelsen advarer: Gylle med plastikrester kan i årevis være blevet spredt på markerne

segments.body: Denmark’s food authority says there is a high risk that slurry containing plastic has contaminated fields linked to a major pig producer, according to documents obtained by DR. The authority believes the issue may have continued for years. The family behind the operation owns 1,400 hectares of land and supplies Danish Crown.

segments.title: What inspectors recorded
segments.body: Inspection records say the company told the authority that it had spread feed containing plastic on a nearby fallow field after being prohibited from using it. The company’s owner has maintained that pigs did not eat plastic. The authority says it has not found visible plastic in the animals’ faeces.

segments.title: Environmental concerns
segments.body: Researchers cited by DR say small plastic particles may pass through filters and could affect plants, but the extent of any risk to people through food remains uncertain. Lejre Municipality says it has not tested the fields for microplastics and will coordinate with Holbæk Municipality on what happens next.

content.headline: Documents suggest Denmark’s property-valuation appeals rule was designed to curb
content.shortHeadline: Documents show origins of Denmark’s 20% property-appeal rule
content.standfirst: Internal records obtained by DR show officials discussed ways to discourage appeals before the current rule was introduced. The rule generally blocks changes unless an assessment is more than 20% wrong, though the tax minister says errors involving clearly incorrect information may be treated differently.

image.caption: DR’s graphic on documents tracing the origins of the 20% property-appeal rule.

sources.originalTitle: Dokumenter afslører: For 11 år siden lagde topfolk en plan, der har konsekvenser for boligejere i dag

segments.body: Internal documents obtained by DR show that tax officials discussed “appeal-prevention measures” in 2015 while designing Denmark’s property-valuation system. A 20% rule later became part of the system: as a general rule, a homeowner must show that a valuation is more than 20% wrong to succeed in an appeal.

segments.title: A homeowner’s case
segments.body: The rule is under renewed scrutiny after a valuation authority acknowledged that it wrongly assumed a summer-house plot could support far more building than local planning rules allow. The error made the land valuation 16.25% too high, but the authority declined to change it under the threshold. Tax minister Jakob Engel-Schmidt has asked officials to reconsider how the rule applies when information is clearly wrong.

segments.title: Concerns over access to appeal
segments.body: A University of Copenhagen law professor who reviewed parts of the documents for DR said the rule cuts into citizens’ ordinary appeal rights. The documents include redactions, and DR says its request for fuller access has been appealed. The tax ministry says the margin reflects uncertainty in property valuations; 6,305 appeals were received in 2025.

content.headline: Another data breach exposes personal details of 11,000 people in Denmark
content.shortHeadline: New CPR data breach affects 11,000 people
content.standfirst: Unauthorised access to Denmark’s civil register was detected this week, months after an earlier incident exposed data on about 8.8 million people. Authorities say new monitoring stopped the latest breach; police are investigating.

sources.originalTitle: Endnu et CPR-læk med 11.000 personer er blevet opdaget

segments.body: Unauthorised access to personal details held in Denmark’s Central Person Register affected 11,000 people, the digitalisation ministry says. The incident was discovered on Monday and did not include people with protected names and addresses. Police are investigating.

segments.title: A second breach
segments.body: The ministry says new technical monitoring introduced after an incident in October detected and stopped the latest access. The earlier breach exposed details including names, addresses and CPR numbers for about 8.8 million people, including people who were alive, deceased or had moved abroad.

segments.title: Review under way
segments.body: Digitalisation minister Christina Egelund says the register needs modernisation and tighter security. A review of the system, launched after the October incident, is expected to finish before Christmas. A Danish Industry cybersecurity expert called the new breach serious but said the monitoring had worked to stop it.

content.headline: Nationalbank warns Denmark’s future storm-surge losses could more than triple
content.shortHeadline: Denmark’s storm-surge losses could more than triple by 2050
content.standfirst: A Nationalbank analysis estimates that an extreme surge along coasts hit by storm Bodil could cause DKK 4.8bn in damage today, and more than three times that by 2050 in a high-emissions scenario. The current compensation system may not be equipped for the risks.

sources.originalTitle: Fremtidens storme kan efterlade boligejere med voldsomme tab, lyder advarsel

segments.body: An extreme storm surge along the same coasts hit by storm Bodil in 2013 could cause DKK 4.8bn in damage and losses today, the Nationalbank estimates. In a high-emissions scenario, the damage could more than triple by 2050 as rising seas put more buildings and property at risk.

segments.title: Pressure on compensation and lending
segments.body: The Nationalbank warns that the current storm-surge compensation scheme may not have enough funding to cover future losses. If homeowners and businesses receive less compensation, some could struggle to repay loans, creating a credit risk for banks and mortgage lenders. Properties in flood-prone areas could also lose value.

segments.title: Prevention and payment
segments.body: The analysis points to coastal protection and climate adaptation as ways to reduce losses. The insurance industry has called for higher fees and a risk-based contribution system, in which those most exposed pay more. The government has yet to set out what its planned agreement on climate adaptation will mean for future policy.

content.headline: Danish researchers test AI that estimates death risk from a face image
content.shortHeadline: AI model estimates death risk from a patient’s face
content.standfirst: A Danish research team says its model performed 34% better than a standard early-warning score in predicting early death from emergency-room images. It is not in routine use and needs further testing; experts also raise ethical concerns.

sources.originalTitle: Ét billede kan hjælpe med at vurdere din risiko for at dø, viser studie

segments.body: A Danish AI model trained on nearly 28,000 photographs of patients at Herlev Hospital was 34% better than the standard Early Warning Score at predicting early death, a peer-reviewed study in Nature reports. The model assessed patients’ risk at different intervals, from one day to one month.

segments.title: Not ready for routine use
segments.body: The model is not yet being used routinely in hospitals and needs further testing. Researchers say it may detect subtle signs in facial features, but a University of Copenhagen professor cautions that the reasons behind those signals are not yet understood and could be misinterpreted.

segments.title: Ethical questions
segments.body: A researcher at Aarhus University and Silkeborg Regional Hospital raises questions about how staff should balance the AI score with their own assessment and explain the use of patient data. The study’s researchers say the technology could eventually be useful in places with limited access to medical staff, including parts of Greenland.

content.headline: Kerteminde council faces close vote on stopping Odense port expansion planning
content.shortHeadline: Kerteminde council set for close vote on port expansion
content.standfirst: A proposed DKK 2bn expansion of Odense Port could add a million square metres to the fjord area. DR reports that a narrow majority appears likely to vote against continuing planning work, but the result was still pending at the time of reporting.

image.caption: Residents fill Kerteminde town hall ahead of a vote on planning for the port expansion.

sources.originalTitle: Byrådssal fyldt til bristepunktet: Én stemme kan stoppe milliardinvestering

segments.body: Kerteminde council is due to vote on whether to stop planning work for a DKK 2bn expansion of Odense Port. The project would increase the port’s capacity and include about a million square metres of additional area in the fjord, as well as a deeper shipping channel.

segments.title: A narrow margin
segments.body: DR reports that a change in the Social Democrats’ council representation appears to have shifted the balance: 13 councillors are expected to oppose continuing the plans and 12 to support it. Protesters gathered outside the town hall, carrying signs that said the fjord was being killed. The vote’s outcome was not reported in the supplied account.

content.headline: National Museum to cut 23 jobs in latest savings round
content.shortHeadline: Denmark’s National Museum to cut 23 positions
content.standfirst: The museum says 20 staff have been notified of redundancies and three others accepted voluntary severance. It is the second round of job cuts this year, following a decline in visitor numbers and an earlier reduction of 21 posts.

sources.originalTitle: Spareplan koster 23 stillinger på Nationalmuseet

segments.body: Denmark’s National Museum will lose 23 positions in a new cost-cutting round. Twenty employees were told on Thursday that they would be laid off, while three accepted voluntary severance, the museum told news agency Ritzau.

segments.title: A second round this year
segments.body: The museum announced on 3 November that it needed to save between DKK 11m and DKK 13m. It said visitor numbers had fallen. Earlier this year, it cut 21 positions, but the museum said those measures were not enough.

content.headline: Man sentenced to eight months for online threats and hate speech
content.shortHeadline: Horsens man jailed for online threats and hate speech
content.standfirst: A 74-year-old man was convicted over social-media posts that included calls to kill members of parliament and people of another ethnic background, and a statement that no Palestinians should survive. He has 14 days to consider an appeal.

sources.originalTitle: Otte måneders fængsel for trusler og had på sociale medier

segments.body: A 74-year-old man from Horsens has been sentenced to eight months in prison for threats, hate speech and publicly encouraging crime, the prosecution service for Southeast Jutland Police says. The convictions relate to posts made between autumn 2022 and May 2024.

segments.title: Posts cited in the case
segments.body: The man was convicted over a Facebook post calling for the killing of members of parliament and people of a different ethnic background, and a post on X saying that “no Palestinians should survive”. He has 14 days to decide whether to appeal.

content.headline: Andy Taylor’s rock guitar helped define Duran Duran’s sound
content.shortHeadline: Andy Taylor’s guitar gave Duran Duran a harder edge
content.standfirst: The guitarist, who has died aged 65, brought a rock sensibility to the band’s polished pop. His playing helped turn synth-led songs into hits with an appeal beyond the group’s original New Romantic world.

image.caption: Andy Taylor in Maison Rouge Studios in 1984.

sources.originalTitle: Andy Taylor, guitarist in Duran Duran, dies aged 65
Duran Duran were transformed by Andy Taylor’s rock edge – and never quite the same without him

segments.body: Andy Taylor, Duran Duran’s guitarist, has died aged 65. Diagnosed with stage four metastatic prostate cancer in 2018, he disclosed his illness in 2022. The band said his playing brought an “indelible fire and swagger” to the songs that took them around the world.

segments.title: A rock edge in a pop band
segments.body: Taylor’s harder-rock influences set him apart from his bandmates, but his guitar helped give Duran Duran a distinctive sound. The Guardian’s account argues that it also made their synth-heavy pop more accessible to US radio, helping the group become a major British success in America.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s retrospective focuses on Taylor’s musical role: his guitar translated some of Nick Rhodes’s synth ideas into a rock language and, the article argues, gave US radio programmers a familiar point of entry.

content.headline: Novelist’s eclectic Scenes confirms him as a British rap original
content.shortHeadline: Novelist’s genre-hopping Scenes is a confident return
content.standfirst: Eight years after his debut album, the south London rapper packs 25 tracks into a restless, 45-minute record. The review hears sharp writing and a fearless range of styles held together by his distinctive voice.

image.caption: South London rapper Novelist, also known as Kojo Kankam.

sources.originalTitle: Novelist’s first album in eight years has Skepta, skits and soul – and showcases a true British original

segments.body: Scenes moves between grime, soul, jungle, baile funk and skits, refusing to settle into one sound. The Guardian review finds coherence instead in Novelist’s sharp, unsentimental rhymes and his willingness to follow each musical idea wherever it leads.

segments.title: A world beyond the album
segments.body: The release comes with an air freshener and a small driving game set around London and Los Angeles landmarks. The review treats these eccentric extras as part of Novelist’s independent-minded approach, rather than a substitute for the music.

content.headline: The KLF-backed People’s Pyramid turns grief into a public ritual
content.shortHeadline: Birkenhead’s People’s Pyramid makes mourning communal
content.standfirst: At the annual Day of the Dead in Birkenhead, families add bricks containing glazed ashes to a growing monument. The event mixes noise, celebration and reflection, and has become a community its organisers say extends beyond the KLF’s original involvement.

image.caption: Participants carry out the Krossing of the Dark Park at Birkenhead’s Day of the Dead.

sources.originalTitle: ‘My brother was its first body’: would you add your corpse to Birkenhead’s pyramid of dead people?

segments.body: The People’s Pyramid is planned to contain 34,592 bricks, each holding a small portion of someone’s cremated remains. At this year’s ceremony, mourners processed through Birkenhead Park, added new bricks and called out the names of the dead amid music, foghorns and a collective moment of noise.

segments.title: A community built around remembrance
segments.body: For participants, the event offers a recurring place to remember people whose funerals did not feel like the right tribute. Families return each year, and organisers hope the monument may eventually have a permanent home in Birkenhead Park. Funding remains uncertain.

content.headline: The Damned mark 50 years with a ferocious, shape-shifting set
content.shortHeadline: The Damned’s 50th-anniversary show stays gloriously unruly
content.standfirst: With all their surviving original members onstage, the punk veterans ranged from hardcore-speed blasts to goth theatrics and prog detours. The review finds their eclecticism still bound together by the force of the performance.

image.caption: Dave Vanian performs with the Damned at Brighton Dome.

sources.originalTitle: Mwhahaha! After 50 years, the Damned are still an outrageously fun blast of punk, pop and gothic camp

segments.body: Rather than rely on a set of early punk hits, the Damned drew on the many directions their music took afterwards. The Guardian’s Brighton review highlights the hardcore charge of “Love Song”, the horror-show camp of “Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde” and a knowingly expansive “Curtain Call”.

The variety never loosens the show’s grip. At 70, Dave Vanian’s baritone remains striking, while the band attacks even the half-century-old “New Rose” with the urgency of new material. Their longevity, the review suggests, has not tamed their messy, contrarian appeal.

content.headline: Bob Dylan’s voice surprises at 85 as he reworks his songs again
content.shortHeadline: Bob Dylan’s voice is a surprise on his latest UK tour
content.standfirst: Opening another UK leg of his Never Ending Tour, Dylan offered no stage chat and little concession to nostalgia. The review finds imaginative arrangements, an unexpectedly strong voice and moments when the slow pace drifts.

image.caption: Bob Dylan performing in 2023.

sources.originalTitle: Bob Dylan review – at 85, he is in finer voice now than he was 40 years ago

segments.body: Dylan performed from behind a piano, guiding his band through a two-hour set with minimal lighting and no gaps between songs. Familiar material arrived in altered forms: “Tangled Up in Blue” became subdued jazz, while “It Ain’t Me Babe” received a probing, delicate arrangement.

segments.title: A voice with new force
segments.body: The reviewer says Dylan’s voice was the evening’s surprise: robust, powerful and clearer than it had sounded four decades earlier. Some slower songs approached lounge music, but the performance’s lyrical sharpness and a closing “I Shall Be Released” offered a route back to the songs for listeners seeking familiar ground.

content.headline: Morten Harket on Parkinson’s, fame and making a new a-ha-free album
content.shortHeadline: Morten Harket on Parkinson’s, fame and Human Grace
content.standfirst: The a-ha singer says medication side effects have affected his access to singing and guitar, but he describes his Parkinson’s diagnosis as a forceful pause rather than a devastation. His new album also features his daughters on two tracks.

image.caption: a-ha frontman Morten Harket.

sources.originalTitle: a-ha’s Morten Harket: ‘My Parkinson’s diagnosis wasn’t devastating. I have a new appreciation for the human organism’

segments.body: Morten Harket says Parkinson’s medication has affected his ability to sing and play guitar. For Human Grace, he and his collaborators drew on older recordings of his voice. He describes the diagnosis as having stopped his previous life and made him newly appreciative of the body’s “architecture”.

segments.title: Fame and family
segments.body: In the interview, Harket recalls the precarious early days of a-ha in south London, when the band slept in cramped, unsafe accommodation, and reflects on the isolation fame brought. He also explains that his daughters’ contributions to two songs were unplanned, after the tracks seemed to need additional voices.

content.headline: Radie Peat’s solo debut brings old folk songs into striking new forms
content.shortHeadline: Radie Peat’s solo debut makes folk feel newly alive
content.standfirst: The Lankum singer draws on Irish, British and American song traditions for an album shaped around her commanding contralto. Its most adventurous turn recasts a folk tune as a dark, widescreen trip-hop piece.

sources.originalTitle: No Human Tongue Can Tell

segments.body: No Human Tongue Can Tell keeps Radie Peat’s voice at its centre, whether she sings alone or builds choruses from her own layers. The Pitchfork review praises the way her arrangements move across time and tradition without losing the clarity and force of her singing.

segments.title: Tradition with room to change
segments.body: Peat selects songs featuring women negotiating limited choices, then reshapes them with keyboards, concertina and electronic textures. On “The Moon and Stars”, a fiddle tune becomes a trip-hop composition that the review calls the album’s most powerful transformation.

content.headline: Glastonbury’s 2027 headliners are strong names but a cautious choice
content.shortHeadline: Glastonbury’s 2027 bill is short on surprise
content.standfirst: Harry Styles, Billie Eilish and Sam Fender have all earned headline status, the i argues, but their similar career stages make for an underwhelming trio. The piece points to fee limits and the festival’s changing cultural pull as part of the problem.

image.caption: Harry Styles, one of Glastonbury’s announced 2027 Pyramid Stage headliners.

sources.originalTitle: Why Glastonbury can’t get good headliners

segments.body: The i’s critic argues that Glastonbury’s announced Pyramid Stage headliners for 2027—Styles, Eilish and Fender—are individually credible but collectively too similar. The complaint is not about their talent; it is that the festival has chosen little risk or contrast for its most prominent slots.

segments.title: The limits of the booking power
segments.body: The article suggests that Glastonbury’s reported maximum headline fee of £500,000 makes it harder to attract some major touring acts, while the festival’s shared spotlight may also deter established stars. It questions whether the event still has the cultural leverage it once did.

content.headline: Gérard Depardieu will face trial over an alleged rape in Paris
content.shortHeadline: Depardieu ordered to face trial over alleged rape
content.standfirst: An appeals court has upheld a trial over one alleged 2018 rape accusation by actor Charlotte Arnould, while dismissing a second allegation. Depardieu denies wrongdoing and his lawyer is considering a further appeal.

image.caption: Gérard Depardieu at a public appearance.

sources.originalTitle: ⁠Gérard Depardieu to face trial on charges ‌of raping ​actor Charlotte ⁠Arnould

segments.body: The court ruled that Gérard Depardieu should stand trial over an alleged rape of Charlotte Arnould at his Paris home in August 2018. It dismissed a separate allegation said to have occurred the following week. Depardieu denies wrongdoing; the trial date has not been supplied.

segments.title: A separate conviction remains
segments.body: The ruling follows Depardieu’s decision to drop an appeal against a 2025 conviction for sexually assaulting two film-set workers; his 18-month suspended sentence stands. His lawyer called the latest decision a “first victory” for Depardieu while saying the legal process is not finished.

content.headline: Julie Delpy on predatory directors, anger and making her own films
content.shortHeadline: Julie Delpy on anger, agency and a life in film
content.standfirst: The actor, writer and director discusses harassment she says she faced as a young performer, the struggle to receive credit for her work and an industry she believes has tried to keep her down. She is writing six screenplays and says she is excited about what comes next.

image.caption: Julie Delpy at home in West Hollywood.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I was very aggressive. They threw me out of every school’ … Julie Delpy on acting, anger and predatory directors

segments.body: Julie Delpy recalls being asked to undress by a director when she was 13 and describes other experiences of harassment in her career. She says that refusing a powerful director’s advances in her early 20s was followed by word spreading that she was “difficult”.

segments.title: Making work on her own terms
segments.body: Delpy says she contributed ideas and dialogue to Before Sunrise but was frustrated not to receive a writing credit. She later shared a writing credit on Before Sunset. Now writing several screenplays, she says directing and writing let her turn ideas into something tangible, even if not every project succeeds.

content.headline: An Eye for an Eye complicates the story of justice and victimhood in Iran
content.shortHeadline: An Iranian documentary challenges easy ideas of justice
content.standfirst: Tanaz Eshaghian discusses her film about Tahereh, a woman facing execution unless she can meet her husband’s family’s demand for blood money after killing him. The documentary also asks what happens when a woman’s story defies expectations of a “perfect victim”.

image.caption: A still from An Eye for an Eye, directed by Tanaz Eshaghian and Farzad Jafari.

sources.originalTitle: ‘She was so not regretful about killing her husband’: the Iranian film that shines a light on blood money and retributive justice

segments.body: Under Iran’s penal code, the heirs of a murder victim can seek execution, financial compensation or forgiveness. An Eye for an Eye follows Tahereh, who is out on bail after killing her husband and faces execution unless she can raise the compensation demanded by his family.

segments.title: A story that resists simple answers
segments.body: Co-director Tanaz Eshaghian describes a film that does not present Tahereh as an uncomplicated victim: the killing was premeditated, and questions remain about what happened. The documentary also records her account of years of violence and the lack of help she found, while exploring the women on both sides of the case.

content.headline: The Fox review: Olivia Colman leads a wonderfully odd Australian fable
content.shortHeadline: The Fox is a peculiar, playful fable with Olivia Colman
content.standfirst: Dario Russo’s debut sends a talking fox, a troubled couple and a magical hole into a comic spiral. The review enjoys its retro texture and strange transformations, finding more flair here than in a similar recent film.

image.caption: Jai Courtney as Nick and Emily Browning as Kori in The Fox.

sources.originalTitle: The Fox review – talking animals are the least weird thing in this delightfully peculiar comedy

segments.body: In a small Australian town, Nick turns to a talking fox for advice after learning his girlfriend is having an affair. The fox tells him to push her into a magical hole so she will emerge loyal. The Guardian review describes the film as a retro-styled, off-kilter fairytale in which this choice takes the story somewhere increasingly strange.

Olivia Colman voices the fox, while Emily Browning, Jai Courtney and the late Sam Neill help establish the film’s peculiar comic tone. The review praises its visual atmosphere and the way it lets its odd premise unfold without giving away where the plot goes.

content.headline: Amanda Seyfried says You Can See Everything kept her in the dark
content.shortHeadline: Amanda Seyfried on joining You Can See Everything
content.standfirst: Seyfried says Nathan Fielder brought her into the Elizabeth Holmes documentary late, with access to its footage and script tightly controlled. She recalls being filmed as she watched material and wondering how she had ended up inside the project.

image.caption: Amanda Seyfried, who played Elizabeth Holmes in The Dropout and appeared in You Can See Everything.

sources.originalTitle: Amanda Seyfried needed ‘five-factor authentication’ to read You Can See Everything script but still ‘told everyone’

segments.body: Amanda Seyfried says Nathan Fielder first contacted her to discuss her portrayal of Elizabeth Holmes in The Dropout. He later asked her to watch footage for You Can See Everything on camera. She says she could not see the film’s material until she was on set and sometimes received the script only the night before.

Seyfried recalls a dinner with Fielder and Holmes’s partner, Billy Evans, as a “Twilight Zone” experience: she was in his home with Holmes’s children and a camera crew, questioning whether she had become too involved. The documentary has since become a major box-office success in North America.

content.headline: Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie settle their dispute over Château Miraval
content.shortHeadline: Pitt and Jolie settle winery dispute
content.standfirst: The former couple have agreed to end their legal battle over the French winery they once owned together. The terms are confidential; claims about the sale and allegations raised in the dispute remain contested in the reporting.

image.caption: Angelina Jolie and Brad Pitt at the 2015 WSJ Magazine Innovator Awards.

sources.originalTitle: Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie settle years-long legal battle over joint French winery

segments.body: Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie have settled their legal dispute over Château Miraval, according to a joint statement. Both sides have moved to dismiss claims against each other, and the terms of the agreement have not been made public.

Pitt sued after Jolie sold her stake to the Stoli Group, arguing she had broken an agreement not to sell without his consent. Jolie’s counterclaim described alleged abuse and said negotiations over her share foundered over a proposed nondisclosure agreement. Pitt denied the accusations.

content.headline: Wicker review: Olivia Colman’s twig-built romance is strange and funny
content.shortHeadline: Wicker is a strange, funny tale of a husband made of twigs
content.standfirst: An isolated fisherwoman commissions a husband woven from willow in this bawdy, deliberately lopsided fairy tale. The review questions its treatment of the husband’s agency but finds a comic fantasy in its reversal of familiar gender expectations.

image.caption: Olivia Colman’s Fisherwoman pays for a husband woven from wicker.

sources.originalTitle: Wicker is unhinged and sexist. I loved it

segments.body: In Wicker, a fisherwoman played by Olivia Colman pays a basketmaker to create her a husband, played by Alexander Skarsgård, from willow. The resulting romance brings comic absurdity to a village where women’s lives are constrained by convention.

segments.title: A fairy tale with an uneasy bargain
segments.body: The reviewer sees a real tension in the film’s fantasy: the wicker husband’s devotion is written as a joke and a wish fulfilment, but his freedom is difficult to separate from the fact that his wife paid for his creation. The review ultimately enjoys the film’s bawdy tone while arguing its equality message is simpler than its provocation.

content.headline: Don’t Look Back in Anger celebrates Oasis’s reunion but skips the story
content.shortHeadline: Oasis reunion film delivers the euphoria, not the explanation
content.standfirst: Steven Knight’s documentary finds moving scenes of fans around the world and captures the Gallagher brothers’ renewed warmth. But the review says it avoids the central questions of how the reunion happened and what repaired their relationship.

image.caption: A still from Steven Knight’s documentary about the Oasis reunion tour.

sources.originalTitle: Oasis fans’ most important question remains unanswered

segments.body: The film follows Oasis on their 2025 reunion tour, from rehearsals to crowds across several countries. The i review praises the concert footage and the emotional response of fans, including a new generation drawn to songs written decades earlier.

segments.title: The missing middle
segments.body: The documentary moves from a brief history of the band’s split to rehearsals, leaving out much of the intervening years and the reconciliation itself. The review also notes that it barely addresses ticket pricing, leaving its uplifting account of forgiveness without the explanation viewers may be seeking.

content.headline: Tulisa’s The Reckoning turns a tabloid sting into a call for change
content.shortHeadline: Tulisa’s documentary looks beyond the 2013 sting
content.standfirst: The three-part series revisits the Sun on Sunday’s fake-film audition sting and Tulisa Contostavlos’s arrest, then follows her campaign for tighter media regulation. The review praises her advocacy but says the programme’s scope sometimes blurs the questions it wants answered.

image.caption: Tulisa Contostavlos in The Reckoning.

sources.originalTitle: Tulisa: The Reckoning review – it’s hard to believe how far the disgusting drugs set-up went

segments.body: Tulisa: The Reckoning recounts how the singer was drawn into a supposed film audition and then asked to supply drugs to a producer, leading to her arrest and a trial that later collapsed. She says the experience contributed to a suicide attempt in 2013.

segments.title: Campaigning after the scandal
segments.body: The series follows Tulisa as she meets campaigners and politicians and calls for stronger media regulation. The Guardian review values her resolve but says the documentary takes on so much—including other episodes of press intrusion—that it does not fully test what reforms would make the greatest difference. IPSO disputes the programme’s criticism of its independence and handling of complaints.

content.headline: The Hunting Wives finds a wide audience in its Texas culture clash
content.shortHeadline: The Hunting Wives mixes Texas culture wars with soap
content.standfirst: The Netflix drama returns with more sex, scandal and a murder investigation, but its appeal is not limited to its provocative surface. Critics and Texas observers discuss its satire of political performance and the varied views of the state it depicts.

sources.originalTitle: 'It appeals across demographics': How steamy soap The Hunting Wives took on sex, scandal and the US's blue-red divide

segments.body: The Hunting Wives centres on an affluent east Texas community and the affair between East Coast liberal Sophie and conservative powerbroker Margo. Its second season leans into the show’s mix of erotic melodrama, secrets and partisan friction; Netflix has already confirmed a third season.

segments.title: Beyond the political labels
segments.body: Time critic Judy Berman says the show’s characters are preoccupied with political image as much as ethics, helping explain its cross-demographic appeal. Texas Monthly editor Taylor Prewitt adds that the state’s residents often encounter people with opposing views in daily life, a dynamic the show uses for teasing and conflict.

perspectives.body: Prewitt’s Texas-based perspective distinguishes the show’s heightened soap opera from its depiction of a state where people with differing political views often have to interact.

content.headline: Top Gear’s Gordon Ramsay reboot needs more than a famous host
content.shortHeadline: Can Gordon Ramsay give Top Gear a lasting reboot?
content.standfirst: The BBC plans to revive the motoring show in 2028 with Ramsay as lead host, but has not announced his co-presenters. The coverage weighs his car knowledge and television experience against the show’s history of short-lived celebrity-led line-ups.

image.caption: Gordon Ramsay, announced as the lead host of the Top Gear revival.

sources.originalTitle: Top Gear to return with Gordon Ramsay as lead host
‘Big names are notoriously flighty’: will Gordon Ramsay save Top Gear – and can he handle the drudgery?

segments.body: BBC Studios says filming for the new Top Gear will take place next year, with the series due to air in 2028 at Dunsfold aerodrome. Ramsay, a car enthusiast who has appeared on the programme as a guest, will lead the presenting team; the BBC says familiar features including the Stig will return.

segments.title: The challenge is continuity
segments.body: The Guardian’s analysis argues that a big name may attract viewers but may not want the regular work of a long-running magazine show. It says the as-yet-unnamed co-hosts will be crucial to giving the revival stability if Ramsay leaves. Richard Hammond, approached about returning, said he did not want to take Top Gear back to what it was.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s analysis focuses less on Ramsay’s suitability than on the risk of building the reboot around a celebrity who may not stay, and the need for co-presenters who can sustain it.

content.headline: I Am Helen shifts the focus from toxic men to their partners
content.shortHeadline: I Am Helen shows the cost of a partner’s misogyny
content.standfirst: Nicola Coughlan plays a woman whose partner’s coercive behaviour grows out of everyday attitudes as much as overt hostility. The review argues that the drama’s attention to the woman living with that behaviour fills a gap in television’s depictions of toxic masculinity.

image.caption: Nicola Coughlan as Helen and Joe Cole as Steve in I Am Helen.

sources.originalTitle: All men should watch I Am Helen

segments.body: In the latest instalment of Dominic Savage’s anthology, Helen’s partner Steve begins choking her during sex without consent. He then presents himself as the injured party. The i review says the scene’s force lies in how quickly the relationship slips back toward normal after the incident.

segments.title: The ordinary roots of harm
segments.body: The review traces Steve’s changing attitudes to casual workplace talk that tells him he is being denied what he deserves. It argues that Helen’s perspective shifts attention from men’s self-image to the women who bear the consequences, without suggesting that the drama’s subject is simple.

content.headline: Open Secret examines how Russell Brand’s behaviour was enabled
content.shortHeadline: Open Secret looks at the culture that enabled Brand
content.standfirst: The Netflix documentary brings together reporting, testimony and old footage after Brand was sentenced for rape and sexual assault. The review says its most disturbing argument is not that his conduct was invisible, but that it could be treated as acceptable.

image.caption: A still from Netflix’s documentary about Russell Brand.

sources.originalTitle: Netflix’s Russell Brand documentary feels like a horror film

segments.body: Open Secret draws on the Sunday Times investigation and includes accounts from comedians, former partners and people who knew Russell Brand. The i review says the programme’s effect comes from seeing earlier footage alongside later testimony and the conduct described by those interviewed.

segments.title: The wider culture
segments.body: The review argues that Brand’s behaviour was often visible in the entertainment culture around him, where he was framed as a playboy or provocative comic. It says the documentary’s indictment reaches beyond one individual to the institutions and audiences that made his persona commercially acceptable.

content.headline: Prue and Sandi’s South African trip is a joyful travelogue with depth
content.shortHeadline: Prue and Sandi’s South Africa trip finds joy and memory
content.standfirst: Prue Leith returns to places from her childhood with former Bake Off colleague Sandi Toksvig. The review delights in their friendship while noting the series’ franker moments of reflection on apartheid and the changes Leith has witnessed.

image.caption: Prue Leith and Sandi Toksvig in Simon’s Town, South Africa.

sources.originalTitle: Prue and Sandi’s South African Adventure review – you’ll feel lucky to have this joyful show in your life

segments.body: The six-part series follows Leith and Toksvig around South Africa, with Leith sharing memories of the country she left at 20. The Guardian review finds much of its charm in their contrasting rhythms: Leith’s recollections and Toksvig’s exuberant curiosity.

The programme also makes room for conversations about apartheid and the forced removal of a Black woman’s family. Leith says she was raised to oppose apartheid but remains ashamed that she did not understand more of its everyday injustices as a teenager. She is moved by the thriving city she sees today.

content.headline: Keira Knightley and Ambika Mod return to Black Doves’ murky world
content.shortHeadline: Black Doves balances spy-show violence with feeling
content.standfirst: The second season sends Helen searching for her missing handler while Sam faces a new kill list. Knightley, creator Joe Barton and newcomer Ambika Mod discuss the show’s mix of gleeful action, moral unease and unexpectedly intimate character moments.

image.caption: Keira Knightley returns as Helen Webb in Black Doves.

sources.originalTitle: Keira Knightley on Black Doves: ‘The violence is like a video game’

segments.body: Keira Knightley returns as Helen, a spy whose cover is a marriage to a politician, while Ben Whishaw reprises the role of melancholy hitman Sam. In the new season, Helen searches for her missing handler and Sam is given a list of targets in exchange for his freedom.

segments.title: Violence with a human cost
segments.body: Knightley calls the show’s action almost like a video game, but says Barton’s writing brings individual acts of violence into focus. Barton argues that audiences can accept characters who kill if the stories give them compelling personalities and acknowledge the moral grey area.

content.headline: December TV brings new Harry Potter and Pride and Prejudice adaptations
content.shortHeadline: Harry Potter, Austen and more: TV to watch in December
content.standfirst: The month’s television slate ranges from HBO’s new Harry Potter adaptation to Netflix’s Pride and Prejudice, alongside returning comedies, crime stories and dramas. The guide highlights the casts, creative choices and release dates readers can plan around.

image.caption: A promotional image for HBO’s Harry Potter adaptation.

sources.originalTitle: Harry Potter to Pride and Prejudice: 10 of the best TV shows to watch this December

segments.body: The guide’s headline adaptations include HBO’s Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone, planned as the start of a series covering all seven novels, and Netflix’s new Pride and Prejudice, with Emma Corrin as Elizabeth Bennet and Jack Lowden as Darcy.

segments.title: A crowded month of returns
segments.body: The recommendations also include a new Only Murders in the Building case set partly in London, a holiday special centred on Mary Bennet, and new seasons of Emily in Paris and other returning series. The guide provides premiere dates and platforms, though availability varies by territory.

content.headline: Dressmaker turns choosing fabric into an absorbing business sim
content.shortHeadline: Dressmaker makes a business sim out of sewing
content.standfirst: This cosy game asks players to design clothes for demanding customers, manage fabric costs and guide each garment through a sometimes nerve-racking sewing challenge. The review finds both creative freedom and satisfying commercial stakes.

image.caption: A sewing scene from Dressmaker.

sources.originalTitle: Dressmaker review – delightful business sim is a cut above

segments.body: In Dressmaker, players talk to clients, interpret their tastes, choose fabrics and sketch outfits before cutting and sewing the finished pieces. Customers can reject a design if it misses a detail, so the game makes both creative decisions and practical accuracy matter.

segments.title: Comfort with consequences
segments.body: The Guardian review praises the tactile details and the way the game balances its cosy atmosphere with the pressure of keeping a business afloat. Sewing a curved edge can become tense, and a disappointed customer can affect earnings, but new styles and accessories reward good work.

content.headline: GTA VI review: a sprawling crime game with an unexpectedly tender heart
content.shortHeadline: GTA VI finds a love story inside its chaotic world
content.standfirst: Rockstar’s vast fictional Florida supports both extravagant crime and small daily routines, but the review’s emotional centre is the bond between fugitives Jason and Lucia. Its empathy is striking, even as the world remains deliberately explicit and offensive.

image.caption: Jason and Lucia in Grand Theft Auto VI.

sources.originalTitle: Grand Theft Auto VI review – gaming’s most depraved world is now also its greatest love story

segments.body: The Guardian review describes a game so expansive it can feel like a crime film, city simulator and domestic life game at once. Its story follows Jason and Lucia from small-time jobs into increasingly dangerous trouble, while allowing time for shopping, exercise, errands and life together.

segments.title: A different kind of GTA relationship
segments.body: The reviewer says the game makes it difficult not to care about the couple, whose personalities remain distinct from the player’s choices. That connection marks a shift from the series’ usual misanthropy, the review argues, without softening its lewd humour, violence or adult content.

content.headline: GTA VI’s soundtrack makes a case for music beyond the game
content.shortHeadline: GTA VI’s star-packed soundtrack is a world of its own
content.standfirst: A new compilation brings together music from major pop, rap and Latin artists, while the game itself offers hundreds of licensed tracks across 22 radio stations. The review sees Rockstar acting as an influential curator, not simply supplying period colour.

image.caption: French duo Justice, who contributed to Grand Theft Auto VI’s score and soundtrack.

sources.originalTitle: Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album review – even GTA sceptics will warm to this zeitgeisty, star-packed soundtrack

segments.body: The soundtrack album gathers new material from artists including Justice, Dua Lipa and Travis Scott, with a sound that moves between dance-pop, rap and Latin music. The Guardian review says the songs can work independently of the game, while still reflecting its fictional Florida setting.

segments.title: A much larger musical world
segments.body: The album is only a fraction of the game’s music: the review reports 22 stations and 700 licensed songs spanning nine decades. It argues that the game’s changing musical identity, including a stronger focus on clubs and dance music, makes Rockstar an unusually powerful music curator.

content.headline: Why parents should keep Grand Theft Auto VI away from young children
content.shortHeadline: GTA VI is an adults-only game, not a children’s gift
content.standfirst: A Guardian writer who has spent more than 70 hours with the game argues that its 18 rating reflects explicit sex, drug use and violence, not difficulty. The piece urges parents to understand the content before buying it for children.

image.caption: Grand Theft Auto VI, an adults-only game.

sources.originalTitle: Parents: please don’t buy Grand Theft Auto VI for your child

segments.body: The writer describes GTA VI as a detailed and often funny crime game, but says its explicit sexual scenes, drug use and graphic violence make it unsuitable for children. The article contrasts its adult content with a common misunderstanding that an 18 rating signals only a high level of difficulty.

segments.title: Making an informed choice
segments.body: The piece notes that parents may feel a teenager has already encountered more explicit media, but argues that the game’s content can be difficult for younger players to contextualise. It frames the rating as practical guidance rather than a call for a moral panic about adult games.

content.headline: GTA VI’s quiet escapes offer a break from crime and chaos
content.shortHeadline: Five quieter places to explore in GTA VI
content.standfirst: A guide to Leonida’s beaches, trails, zoo and art-filled corners suggests ways to explore the game beyond its crimes and missions. The recommendations also point to the detail that makes its open world inviting.

image.caption: Mount Kalaga in Grand Theft Auto VI.

sources.originalTitle: Seven beautiful places to visit in GTA VI, from mountains trails to an afternoon at the zoo

segments.body: The Guardian’s guide recommends Mount Kalaga for trails and birdwatching, a Vice City zoo for a slower stroll, and beaches and islands for views, wildlife and time away from the city. The writer also points out a museum and an unusual public artwork that may prompt further player investigation.

content.headline: Hera’s close-up images reveal the aftermath of Nasa’s asteroid impact test
content.shortHeadline: Hera reveals the aftermath of Nasa’s asteroid impact test
content.standfirst: Images of Dimorphos show that Nasa’s 2022 collision changed the asteroid’s shape and motion. The findings could help scientists work out how to make future deflection missions more reliable.

image.caption: Hera images show a crater across Dimorphos after Nasa’s 2022 impact test.

sources.originalTitle: Nasa knocked an asteroid off course. New closeup photos shed light on aftermath

segments.title: A crater across the asteroid
segments.body: The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft has returned the first close-up images of Dimorphos, four years after Nasa deliberately crashed its Dart spacecraft into the asteroid. The pictures show the impact flattened one face into a crater spanning the asteroid’s width; Dimorphos is also tumbling, and hundreds of small boulders surround it and its larger companion, Didymos.

segments.title: From a successful test to a reliable defence
segments.body: Dart shortened the time Dimorphos takes to orbit Didymos by about 33 minutes, but how much material the impact displaced and how the asteroid responded remained open questions. Hera’s observations can help researchers improve calculations for a future deflection mission; neither asteroid posed a danger to Earth.

segments.title: More measurements to come
segments.body: Hera is expected to move closer and release two small satellites, one equipped with radar to look inside Dimorphos. Researchers say the asteroid’s structure matters: a loosely bound pile of rocks may react differently to an impact than a more solid body. Detecting a threatening asteroid early would also give more time to respond.

content.headline: Survey finds sharp fall in hormonal contraception use among young women
content.shortHeadline: Hormonal contraception use falls among young women
content.standfirst: New Natsal-4 findings point to growing concerns about hormonal methods, alongside gaps in effective contraception. Doctors say online claims and limited access to balanced advice may be contributing factors.

sources.originalTitle: Contraceptive pill usage in Great Britain fell drastically in last decade, research finds

segments.body: Use of hormonal contraception among women aged 16 to 24 in Great Britain fell from 64.6% to 50.3% over the past decade, according to the Natsal-4 survey published in The Lancet. Almost one in five women at risk of an unintended pregnancy said they were not using effective contraception.

segments.title: Concerns and access to advice
segments.body: Doctors cited online claims about hormones, including unsupported suggestions that contraception causes lasting damage to fertility, as one possible influence on choices. The survey also found that the share of women aged 16 to 44 who said they definitely did not want children had more than doubled. Dr Zara Haider of the College of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare said service cuts and limited sex education may also contribute to gaps in access.

content.headline: S&P weighs Nvidia downgrade after CEO upheaval raises governance concerns
content.shortHeadline: S&P weighs Nvidia downgrade after CEO turmoil
content.standfirst: The rating agency is reviewing Nvidia’s AA credit rating after Jensen Huang’s abrupt departure and return exposed concerns about oversight and succession planning. A downgrade could also make borrowing more expensive for AI infrastructure firms.

image.caption: Jensen Huang at an event in Taiwan in May.

sources.originalTitle: S&P considers Nvidia credit downgrade over governance and ‘key man’ risks
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang apologizes to staff: ‘I made some terrible mistakes’
Jensen Huang broke Nvidia’s code of conduct, and his employees may not forget it

segments.title: A review with wider financial stakes
segments.body: S&P Global Ratings says it may lower Nvidia from AA to AA-, citing weak executive oversight, a lack of succession planning and the company’s reliance on Huang. The review is expected to conclude within 90 days. Nvidia would remain investment-grade, but a downgrade could raise its borrowing costs.

segments.title: Why lenders are watching
segments.body: Nvidia backs financing for infrastructure companies with weaker credit of their own, so higher borrowing costs could spread beyond the chipmaker. The company previously planned, with six financial institutions, up to $500bn in AI infrastructure financing; lenders had already sought larger guarantees before the CEO upheaval, according to S&P’s reporting.

segments.title: A question of company culture
segments.body: Huang has acknowledged violating Nvidia’s code of conduct but said that a breach does not automatically mean an employee is dismissed. Matt Plass of LRN, cited by TechCrunch, argues that when rules appear not to apply equally, the greater risk may be damage to employees’ trust and pride in the company.

perspectives.body: LRN’s Matt Plass says a code of conduct reflects workplace culture: when senior leaders break one without consequence, employees may feel embarrassed or angry, even if there is no immediate business cost.

content.headline: 1Password says breach exposed customer contact details, not password vaults
content.shortHeadline: 1Password says customer vaults were not breached
content.standfirst: A hacker accessed internal systems through an employee’s compromised GitHub account and took some customer information, the company says. The number affected and how the attacker gained access remain unclear.

sources.originalTitle: 1Password breach leaked customer names and emails, but not passwords
1Password said hackers broke into its internal systems, but customer passwords are safe

segments.body: 1Password says an attacker used access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account to push malicious code to internal systems and download some customer data. Names and email addresses were among the information taken. The company says customer password vaults, passwords and secret keys were not accessed.

segments.title: Questions remain for customers
segments.body: The company has not said how many people were affected. TechCrunch reported it had not received answers on whether affected customers had been notified or how the attacker first gained access. 1Password says it disabled the compromised account, rotated affected credentials and extended the length of codes sent by email; it warns customers to watch for phishing attempts.

perspectives.body: TechCrunch reported that the company had not answered whether customers were notified, how many accounts were affected or how the attacker obtained access to the employee account.

content.headline: US court says Amazon must handle recalls of hazardous third-party products
content.shortHeadline: Amazon must handle recalls of hazardous products, court rules
